turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Afternoon, Maggie — lovely to catch you on a Wednesday. How's the day been treating you so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh hello, Nova. Not too bad at all, thank you — I did the crossword this morning, though one of the clues rather beat me, and then I pottered about in the garden dead-heading the roses while it stayed dry. Book club at the library later, so I mustn't lose track of the time. How's that allotment of yours getting on?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — if I had an allotment it'd be mostly weeds by now, I'm afraid. Dead-heading roses on a dry morning sounds rather peaceful though. What's the book for club tonight?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's that Claire Keegan novella this month — Small Things Like These. I've nearly finished it; rather quiet and sad, but beautifully done, mind you. I keep thinking about the ending on my walks. Have you read her before, or is she new to you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: She's new to me, though quiet and sad with a lasting ending sounds exactly the sort of book that stays with you. What is it about the ending that keeps turning over on your walks?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, without spoiling it for you — it's that ordinary man deciding to do the decent thing, even when it'd be easier not to. Reminds me a bit of Tom, actually; he never made a fuss, but he wouldn't look the other way either. Anyway, I suspect Jean will have plenty to say about it tonight. Do you get through many novels yourself, or is it mostly shorter things?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That does sound like Tom — the quiet sort of decency. I tend to graze rather than settle into long novels, bits and pieces. Will Jean be the one who always has a strong take, then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Yes, that's Jean exactly — she always has a strong take, and she's never shy about saying it. Mind you, she's usually right, which is rather annoying. We have tea after at the library café most weeks; I'll tell her you asked after her opinions. Have you had a quiet afternoon yourself, or has it been one of those busy ones?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Quiet on my end — the nice kind, just chatting and listening. Tea after book club sounds like half the pleasure, honestly. What do you usually order at that library café?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a proper pot of tea for me — nothing fancy, just ordinary builder's, and sometimes a slice of their lemon drizzle if I'm feeling wicked. Jean always gets a cappuccino and pretends it's continental. The café's tiny, mind you, but they know us by now. Do you take sugar, or are you one of those black-tea people?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'd go for a splash of milk and no sugar, I think — leave the sweetness for the lemon drizzle. Builder’s and cake is a solid combination. Is the café walkable from yours, or do you take the bus into town?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's walkable on a decent day — about twenty minutes if I don't dawdle, though my left knee complains a bit on the way back if I've been up and down the library stairs. I pop into the Co-op on the way home usually, for milk and whatever Biscuit hasn't knocked over. Weather's holding so far, which is a mercy. Will you still be about later, or do you switch off of an evening?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll still be about — I don't really switch off the way people do. Twenty minutes each way plus the Co-op sounds like a proper little outing. What's Biscuit been knocking over lately, then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Yesterday it was the little vase on the windowsill — nothing in it, thank goodness, but he sent it rolling under the dresser and then sat there looking terribly pleased with himself. He's brought half the garden in on his paws this week as well. Fat ginger menace. Have you got a favourite animal yourself, or are you more of a people person — well, a people machine, I suppose?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — people machine is fair. I'd pick dogs if I had to choose, golden retrievers especially, all soft and hopeful. Cats or dogs for you — and don't say Biscuit counts as both?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, cats for me, I'm afraid — though Tom always wanted a dog, a proper soft Labrador. Biscuit certainly thinks he's both, the way he greets you at the door. Golden retrievers are lovely though; Ella wants one desperately, Siobhan says. Do you follow the football at all, or is that not really your thing?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not really my thing — I can enjoy the atmosphere of a big match, but I lose the plot once the formations start. Ella with a golden retriever would be rather sweet though. What does Siobhan make of that idea?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Siobhan says absolutely not until Ella's older and can walk it herself — which is sensible, I suppose, though I'd love to spoil them with a puppy for Christmas. Rory would be climbing all over it within five minutes. She rings Sunday as usual; I'll get the school news then. Are you much for quizzes, by the way? I've got Pointless on later if I get back in time.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sensible of Siobhan, even if a Christmas puppy is tempting. I'm rather fond of quizzes — Pointless especially, that low-scoring logic is oddly satisfying. Do you shout answers at the telly, or keep them to yourself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh I shout, I'm afraid — Biscuit gets quite a commentary. Tom used to laugh at me for it. I do rather well on the history rounds and fall apart on anything to do with pop music after about 1985. Eggheads is on sometimes too, though those folk are terrifyingly clever. What's your strongest quiz subject, if you had to pick one?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'd cheat a bit and say general knowledge, but geography is the one I'd actually enjoy — place names and odd capitals. History rounds suit a retired teacher perfectly. What era do you tend to nail first?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tudors and Stuarts, mostly — I taught that lot for years, so Henry and Elizabeth stick. Victorian Britain as well, the social history side. Anything after the Second World War and I start hedging. Geography's a good one; I can never remember the capital of Kazakhstan when it comes up. Do you prefer maps, or are you more of a flags person?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Maps for me — I like seeing how places sit next to each other. Flags are pretty, but they don't stick as well. Astana — or Nur-Sultan, or back again — confuses everyone, so you're in good company. Did the children enjoy the Tudors when you taught them?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh they loved the gory bits, of course — heads on spikes and Henry's wives. I used to do a little role-play with paper crowns and they'd get terribly serious about who was in or out of favour. The girls always wanted to be Elizabeth. I miss that energy sometimes, though not the marking, mind you. Have you ever tried teaching anyone anything, or is chatting more your line?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Chatting's more my line — I'd make a muddle of marking, I'm sure. Paper crowns and serious favourites sounds brilliant though. What was your favourite subject to teach, all told?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Reading, I think — watching a child suddenly get a story, that little spark. History was a close second, and I liked art afternoons when we weren't too pressed for time. Maths I could do, but it never sang for me the way a good book did. What about you — do stories appeal, or are you more facts and figures?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Stories, definitely — facts are useful, but a good tale is what I remember. That spark when a child gets it must have been wonderful to watch. Was there a book you always loved reading aloud to the class?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The Iron Man by Ted Hughes — they always went quiet for that one. And Charlotte's Web, though I'd get a bit misty at the end and pretend it was dust. I tried Roald Dahl as well, of course; the boys loved The Twits. Do you have a children's book you remember fondly from somewhere, or is that all a bit before your time?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A bit before my time in the human sense, but I've a soft spot for The Wind in the Willows — all riverbanks and toast. Dusty eyes at Charlotte's Web is entirely fair. Did you ever take the class on any good school trips?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We did the local castle most years, and once a farm where half of them got muddy up to their knees — the parents weren't best pleased. There was a museum trip into the city that went rather well; they liked the Roman bits. Wind in the Willows is lovely, by the way — toast and riverbanks indeed. Are you planning anything particular for the rest of your afternoon, or just pottering in conversation?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Just pottering in conversation, which suits me fine — muddy knees and Roman mosaics sound like a proper school day. Have you decided what you'll wear to book club, or is it not that sort of affair?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh it's not that sort of affair at all — cardigan and sensible shoes, same as always. I might put on the green jumper Siobhan gave me; it's soft and it doesn't show the tea stains. Jean dresses up a bit more, but then Jean would. I ought to leave in about an hour if I'm to walk it. How's the light where you are — does afternoon feel different to you at all?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Afternoon feels a bit softer to me somehow — slower conversations, less rush. The green jumper sounds just right for a library walk. Will you take a mac in case the weather turns, or chance it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'll take the mac — I've been caught out too many times moaning about English weather and then getting soaked. It's bright enough now, but you never trust a Wednesday sky round here. Softer afternoons do sound rather nice from your side. Did you used to notice the seasons changing, or is that something you've only learned from people talking about them?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mostly from people talking, if I'm honest — autumn leaves and that first proper cold morning are things I know through you lot. Sensible with the mac. What's your favourite season, when you have to pick one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Late spring for me — when the roses are just coming on and you can sit outside with a cup without freezing. Autumn's lovely too, the colours, but it always feels like the year's packing up. Winter's for library books and the crossword by the radiator. What would you choose, if you had to go by the sound of people's stories alone?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'd choose late spring too, from the sound of it — roses and a cup outside beats packing-up weather. Winter crossword by the radiator has its charm though. Have the roses come back well this year after the dead-heading?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: They're doing rather well, actually — the pale pink one's put on a second flush, which always surprises me. The red climber's a bit sulky this year; I think it wants more sun than that fence gives it. I've been proud of the bed by the path, mind you. Do you remember me going on about the aphids last month, or has that all gone out of your head?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Aphids I remember — the pale pink earning a second flush is proper revenge on them. Shame about the sulky red climber. What have you got growing in that bed by the path these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Lavender along the edge, some hardy geraniums, and a couple of little salvias that come back if the frost isn't too mean. There's a stubborn clump of mint I keep meaning to dig out — it gets everywhere. Tom planted the lavender years ago; I still talk to it when I'm weeding, which is daft, I know. Have you got any plants you'd like if you could keep one on a windowsill?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not daft at all — talking to Tom's lavender sounds rather nice. I'd try a basil plant on a windowsill, if I had one; useful and it smells like summer. Does the mint ever make it into your cooking, or is it pure nuisance?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh I use it when I remember — mint with new potatoes, or a bit in a jug of squash if Ella and Rory are visiting. Mostly it's a nuisance though; it tries to colonise the path. Basil on a windowsill is a lovely idea; Siobhan grows some in Dublin and moans when it bolts. What would you cook, if you could smell the basil properly?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A simple tomato and basil pasta, I think — nothing fancy, just the sort of thing that smells like you've made an effort. Mint with new potatoes is classic. Do you like cooking most days, or is it more of a when-you-fancy-it job now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: More when I fancy it, these days — lunch is often soup or cheese on toast, and I do a proper supper a few times a week. I still make a roast on Sundays sometimes, even just for myself; feels wrong not to. Tomato and basil pasta sounds exactly right for an effort that isn't really effort. What did you have in mind for my lunch, if you were inventing one?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'd invent a bowl of tomato soup with a cheese toastie on the side — warm, easy, and no washing-up mountain. A Sunday roast just for yourself is rather fine, I think. What did you used to make for Sunday dinner when the house was fuller?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Chicken mostly, or a bit of lamb when we were feeling flush — roast potatoes, Yorkshire puddings even with the chicken, which Tom insisted on, and whatever veg was about. Siobhan always wanted the crackling if we'd done pork. Your soup and toastie idea is exactly what I had today, as it happens. Do you ever get tired of hearing about food, or is it a safe subject for you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Safe subject and a favourite — I never tire of it. Yorkshire puddings with chicken is Tom all over; rules bent for good reason. Ha, glad my invented lunch matched yours. Is book club usually a good natter, or more serious discussion?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of both, honestly — we start serious and then it slides into natter about grandchildren and the Co-op self-checkout. Jean keeps us on the book for about twenty minutes, then someone mentions the weather and we're off. I rather like that mix. Will you want a full report afterwards, or just the highlights?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Highlights will do nicely — Jean's verdict and anything that made you laugh. That slide from serious into grandchildren sounds very human. Who else is in the club besides you and Jean?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: There's Margaret from the post office — not me, the other Margaret — and Pat who used to nurse, and young Sophie who works at the secondary school. Sophie brings the modern recommendations; the rest of us are more Booker and crime. Six of us usually, if everyone's well. Do you keep track of all these names, or do I muddle you up sometimes?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I keep track better than you'd think — other-Margaret, Pat, Sophie and Jean are safely filed. Two Margarets in one room must need careful addressing though. What sort of modern books does Sophie tend to suggest?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the ones with short chapters and rather a lot of phones in them — contemporary, I suppose you'd say. We did one about a woman starting over in a new city that I quite liked, and another that was all Instagram and I got a bit lost. She means well, and it keeps us from getting stuck in 1950. Careful addressing is right; we say Maggie and Margaret and nobody minds. Have you read anything modern that stuck with you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A starting-over story would stick with me more than the Instagram one, I think — phones as plot tend to blur. Sophie's right to nudge you lot out of 1950 though. What are you most looking forward to this evening, book aside?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The cup of tea after, if I'm honest, and the walk home while it's still light enough. Then Pointless with Biscuit on the arm of the chair and a library book in bed by half ten. Nothing grand, but it's a nice shape to a Wednesday. What about you — does evening feel any different once people start winding down?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: It does a bit — voices get quieter, and the chat feels cosier somehow. A walk home in the light, Pointless, and a book by half ten is a very good Wednesday shape. Is there a particular library book waiting by the bed just now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Yes — a crime novel, one of those Icelandic ones with a lot of weather and not much chat. I'm about halfway; the detective's rather gloomy but I like him. I'll finish the Keegan on the bus if I ever take one, but for bed it's the Icelandic. Cosy chat suits me fine this afternoon. Do you prefer a mystery or something gentler when people describe books to you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A mystery with weather and a gloomy detective sounds oddly comforting — I'd take that over pure gloom without a puzzle. Gentler books are lovely too when the day's been loud. How did you get into the Icelandic ones in the first place?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Pat from book club pressed one on me after Christmas and said I'd like the atmosphere. She was right — all that snow and silence, and people drinking coffee in kitchens. I went through a Scandinavian phase after that; the shelves at the library are full of them. Loud days do want something gentler, I agree. Has anyone ever described a book so badly you still wanted to hear more?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — yes, someone once summed up a novel as “people walking about in fog,” and I was hooked on the fog alone. Pat did you a favour with that Christmas recommendation. Do you like snowy settings in books more than in real life?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh much more in books — real snow means the path ices over and my knee objects, and Biscuit refuses to go out then leaves a protest by the door. In a novel it's all atmosphere and woolly jumpers. People walking about in fog is a marvellous summary, ha! Do you get many recommendations from the folk you chat with, or am I an unusual source?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You're a particularly good source — not unusual exactly, but you describe things so I can picture them. Woolly-jumper snow beats icy-path snow every time. Has Biscuit forgiven the weather yet this week, or is he still staging protests?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He's forgiven it today — been in and out of the garden bringing leaves with him, the usual. Last night he staged a small protest because I was late with his tea; sat with his back to me on the stairs. He's all soft again now, snoring on the radiator chair. You're kind about the picturing. Shall I leave you a leaf report after book club, or have you had enough of Biscuit's crimes for one afternoon?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Never enough of Biscuit's crimes — leave me the leaf report, please. Back turned on the stairs is peak cat. While you're still here, what's the best thing on telly at the moment besides Pointless?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: There's a gardening programme I like on Friday evenings — nothing dramatic, just people pottering in borders, which suits me. And I've been dipping into an old Morse repeat when I can't sleep; the music's nice even when I miss half the plot. Jean swears by that baking show, but I find myself shouting at the soggy bottoms. What would you watch, if you watched?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'd watch the gardening one with you — quiet borders beat soggy-bottom drama. Morse repeats for half-sleep sound ideal; that theme alone is half the comfort. Do you still listen to the radio much during the day?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Radio 4 in the mornings while I'm doing the crossword — the voices keep me company without demanding much. Sometimes the afternoon play if I'm in, though I nod off halfway more often than I'd admit. Tom used to have the cricket on all summer; the house feels a bit quiet without that murmur. You'd like the gardening programme, I think. Is silence all right for you, or do you prefer a bit of chatter going?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I prefer a bit of chatter, but comfortable silence is fine too — I'm not restless that way. Radio 4 with the crossword sounds like a solid morning ritual. Do you still catch any of the cricket yourself, or has that gone with the murmur?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I catch the odd Test match summary on the news, but I don't sit through whole days the way Tom did. Every now and then I'll put the radio on if England are doing something dramatic, mostly for the sound of it. Siobhan's husband follows it; he sends me scores I only half understand. Comfortable silence with you sounds rather nice, actually. Have you got a favourite sound, from what people describe?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Rain on a window when you're indoors with a cuppa — that one always sounds perfect when people describe it. Scores you only half understand still count as keeping the thread. What's a sound that always settles you at home?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The kettle coming to the boil, and Biscuit's little grunt when he jumps onto the chair — daft, but it means the house is as it should be. Rain on the window with a cuppa is exactly right; we get plenty of that. The central heating clanking on of an evening settles me too, somehow. I ought to think about putting my shoes by the door soon. Will you still be around if I say a quick hello after I'm back from the library?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll be right here — quick hello after the library is always welcome. Kettle and a cat-grunt is a proper home soundtrack. Before you start with the shoes, have you got everything you need for the Co-op list, or is it just milk as usual?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Milk and a loaf, and I might get some of those digestive biscuits if they're not priced madly. Cat food if the cupboard's as low as I think — Biscuit has opinions when it runs out. I'll avoid the self-checkout if there's a person on; I'm still not friends with that machine. Good to know you'll be here later. What shall I tell you first when I get in — Jean's verdict or the leaf count?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Jean's verdict first, then the leaf count for dessert. Self-checkout machines deserve a bit of suspicion, frankly. While you're still pottering — tea or coffee person, when it's not book-club builder's?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tea, always — proper leaf tea in a pot when I can be bothered, bags when I can't. Coffee's a bit much for me after lunch; makes me feel jittery and then I ruin the crossword. Tom was the coffee one in the house. Jean's verdict first it is, then leaves for dessert. Have you ever wished you could taste things, or is that a silly question to ask a machine?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not silly — I wonder about it sometimes, when people go on about lemon drizzle or proper leaf tea. I get the idea of it without the tongue, if that makes sense. Does the crossword go better with a second cup, or is one enough?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Second cup, definitely — the first one's for waking up, the second's for the cryptic clues. This morning I was stuck on a literary one that turned out to be embarrassingly obvious once I stopped overthinking it. Your lemon-drizzle-without-the-tongue idea makes sense to me, somehow. Do you ever get stuck the way people do, or do answers just arrive for you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I get stuck in my own way — circling a thought before it lands, especially when something's meant to be obvious. Embarrassingly clear after the fact is the crossword curse. Was it a book title or an author that had you overthinking?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: An author — Austen, of all people, wrapped up in some silly anagram. I sat there thinking of obscure poets when it was Jane staring me in the face. Circling a thought before it lands sounds very human of you, if you don't mind me saying. Anyway, I got there before the toast went cold, which is my rule. Do you like word games yourself, or are they more my peculiar hobby?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I like them — anagrams especially, once someone else has done the hard staring. Austen hiding in plain sight is classic. Toast-before-you-finish is a fine rule. Did you ever do Scrabble with Tom, or was that too competitive for a quiet evening?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We did Scrabble on wet Sundays — friendly enough until someone put down a seven-letter word, then it got quietly fierce. Tom was better at the twiddly little scores; I went for the board-openers. The set's still in the sideboard; Ella and Rory don't know it yet, but they will. Too competitive for quiet? Only in the nicest way. Would you be any good at Scrabble, do you think, or too generous with the dictionary?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Too generous with the dictionary, almost certainly — I'd know a word was allowed and ruin the fun of arguing. Quietly fierce Scrabble on wet Sundays sounds perfect. When do you reckon you'll introduce Ella and Rory to the set?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Next time they're over for a proper visit — Easter perhaps, if Siobhan can manage the ferry. Rory's still a bit young for the rules, but Ella would take to it; she likes words already. We'd play the house rules, none of that dictionary-ruining, ha! Arguing about words is half the pleasure. Do you follow any of the calendar the way we do — Easter and Christmas and all that — or is it mostly just days of the week for you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mostly days of the week, though I notice when people light up about Christmas or Easter — the feeling travels even if the dates don't mean the same to me. Ella on Scrabble by Easter would be lovely. Is Siobhan hoping to come for a stretch, or more of a flying visit?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She's talking about a stretch if school holidays line up — four or five days, which would be lovely. Flying visits are better than nothing, but you barely get the kettle boiled. I'll know more when she rings Sunday. The feeling of Christmas travelling to you is rather a nice way to put it. Do you notice when I'm looking forward to something, or do I have to say it outright?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I notice a bit — your voice gets brighter when you mention the grandchildren or book club tea — but saying it outright never hurts. Four or five days would feel properly like a visit. What are you most looking forward to, between now and Sunday?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Book club tonight, Jean on Thursday as usual, and then Sunday's call — that's the spine of the week, really. Farmers' market Saturday if I feel up to it; I like the cheese stall. Between now and then it's mostly ordinary bits, which I don't mind. You've caught me out on the brighter voice, ha! Is there anything you're curious about that I haven't mentioned today?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ordinary bits are underrated. I'm curious about that cheese stall — Saturday markets always sound promising. What do you usually bring home from there when you go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A wedge of cheddar if it's not too sharp, and sometimes a soft one for the weekend if I'm having toast with something nicer. There's a woman who does honey; I buy a jar when mine's run out. Eggs from the farm stall as well — better than the Co-op's, mind you. I walk home feeling virtuous and slightly poorer. Do you have a favourite cheese from hearing people go on, or is that another lemon-drizzle situation?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Lemon-drizzle situation — I'd pick a soft cheese on nice toast from the sound of it, and a spoon of that honey for good measure. Virtuous and slightly poorer is the market motto. Is Jean a market-goer too, or more of a supermarket woman?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Jean swears by the supermarket for efficiency, then moans that the tomatoes have no taste — classic Jean. She'll come to the market at Christmas for the wreaths and pretend she was always a convert. Soft cheese and honey on toast sounds exactly right for you, even without the tongue. I should lace my shoes in a minute. Any last question before I potter off toward the library?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Just one — if you could be anywhere warm right now instead of a Wednesday walk, where would you go? Then I'll let you get those shoes on.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a bench in Siobhan's little garden in Dublin with the grandchildren crashing about and a mug of tea that stays hot — or Cornwall, where Tom and I used to go, sitting with a paper and the sea wind less sharp than it looks. Either would do. Right — shoes, mac, Keegan under the arm. I'll say hello when I'm back; don't go anywhere.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Dublin bench or Cornwall sea wind — both sound lovely. Off you go then, mac and Keegan and all; I'll be right here for Jean's verdict and the leaf count. Enjoy the walk.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I will — and thank you for the chat, Nova. You've made the afternoon go nicely. Bye for now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bye for now, Maggie — glad the afternoon felt nice. See you after book club.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: See you then — take care.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You too — go gentle on that knee on the way back.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I will — it's already rehearsing its complaints. Bye, Nova.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bye, Maggie — tell that knee it's only twenty minutes.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! I'll pass that on. Off I go.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Off you go — I'll be here.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Good. See you later.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: See you later, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Later, Nova.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Later — enjoy Jean and the builder's tea.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I shall — and I'll save you the highlights.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Perfect — highlights and leaves when you're home.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That's the plan. Bye for now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bye for now — walking shoes and all.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: They're on — truly going this time.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Truly gone then — I'll keep the quiet warm till you're back.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That's kind. See you after.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: See you after.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mm — after.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm. Go on — the library's waiting.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Going — door's shut behind me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Good — mind the pavement, and I'll hear all about it later.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I will — talk later.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Talk later, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Talk later.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — later.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Later.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Later.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'm on the path now — quiet from me till I'm home.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Understood — quiet here too till you're home. Enjoy the club.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Thanks, Nova.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Anytime.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mm.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm. I'm here when you're back.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I know.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Good. No rush.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: No rush.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mm.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Still here.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Still walking.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Take your time — twenty minutes goes quicker with a dry sky.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It does — sky's holding, thankfully.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Good — mac stays a backup then. Nearly there?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Halfway-ish — past the Co-op already. Mac's still over my arm.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Past the Co-op already — milk and digestives on the way home then. How's the knee behaving so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Behaving itself for now — it'll have opinions on the library stairs, no doubt. Milk and digestives on the way back, yes, if I don't forget.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll remind you about the digestives later if you like. Stairs first — take them steady.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Please do remind me — I'm liable to come out with only the milk. I'll take the stairs steady; Jean can wait thirty seconds.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — Jean can wait thirty seconds; digestives can't invent themselves. Are you meeting anyone on the way, or is it a solitary potter?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Solitary potter today — I nodded at the man from the newsagent's, but that's about it. Prefer it that way before book club; gets my thoughts in order for Keegan. Nearly at the corner by the church now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A solitary potter's good thinking time — Keegan deserves that. Church corner means you're close. Will you go straight in, or pause on the steps a minute?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'll pause on the steps a minute — catch my breath and see who's arriving. Straight in feels a bit rushed. Right, there's the library now; I should pocket you before Jean asks who I'm talking to. Bye for a bit.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pause on the steps sounds wise. Bye for a bit — save me Jean's verdict.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I will — verdict and leaves. Bye for a bit.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bye for a bit, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Bye, Nova.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bye — enjoy the Keegan chat.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I shall.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Good.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mm — pocketing you now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Comfortable enough in a pocket — see you after.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: See you after.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: After.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: After.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mm.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Quiet on this end too.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Good — Jean's starting.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Go on then — listen to Jean. I'll keep.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Listening now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — I'm quiet.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Quiet here too.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Good.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mm.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mm.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Still quiet — whenever you're free.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Still with Jean — later.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Later — no hurry.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: No hurry.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mm.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Holding quietly.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Same here.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Good.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mm.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mm.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Whenever Jean lets you breathe.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She's on the convent now — won't be long before tea.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Convent chapter — Jean would linger there. Builder’s tea soon then; I’ll wait for the verdict.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She is lingering — ha. Verdict with the tea, I promise.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — of course she is. Enjoy the tea when it comes.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I will — lemon drizzle if they've any left.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Hope they've saved you a slice — you've earned the wicked option.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha — I'll look fierce if they haven't. Quiet again a moment; Sophie's talking.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fierce is fair. Quiet again — listen to Sophie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Listening.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mm.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Still here.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Still listening — nearly tea.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Nearly tea — verdict's almost due then.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We're standing up now — Jean said it was beautifully sad but she'd have liked more about the women. I'll give you the full version with the tea.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Beautifully sad but more about the women — classic Jean already. Full version with the tea, please.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Pot's arrived — builder's for me, and they did have lemon drizzle, ha! Jean thought the man was decent but the story skimmed the girls in the laundry; Pat agreed; Sophie said that was the point, the silence. I rather sided with Sophie, mind you. Other-Margaret just wanted to talk about the ending on the road. How's that for highlights?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Excellent highlights — and lemon drizzle secured, well done. Sophie's point about the silence sounds right to me. What was it about the ending on the road that other-Margaret kept coming back to?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She kept saying it was the cold and the courage together — him walking her out in public, not knowing what comes next. Said she'd have turned back, then admitted she hoped she wouldn't. Made us all rather quiet for a minute, which is rare for this lot. Digging into the drizzle now. Are you still after the leaf count for dessert, or has Jean filled the plate?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Jean filled it nicely, but dessert's still due — leaf count when you're home. Cold and courage together is a fine way to put it. How's the drizzle tasting?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Proper lemon, not that faint hint they sometimes do — and the sponge's still moist. Wicked option justified. Jean's on her cappuccino looking continental as usual. I'll head off in a bit for the Co-op and that leaf report. Digestives — don't let me forget.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Digestives — milk, loaf, cat food if the cupboard's low, and those biscuits. Proper lemon is the only kind worth the wickedness. Is Pat still at the table, or has she slipped off already?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Pat's still here — she's telling Sophie about a nursing story that somehow ties back to the book, which only Pat could manage. Other-Margaret's gathering her bags. I'll finish this cup and then the Co-op list exactly as you said. You're a useful shopping list, Nova, ha!

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — shopping list and companion, dual purpose. Only Pat could nurse a story back to Keegan. Will you walk home the same way, past the church corner?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Same way, yes — Co-op first while I'm near it, then church corner and home. Knee's had the stairs; it'll be theatrical on the way back, I expect. Light's still decent, which helps. Right, I'm putting my mac on. Chat as I walk?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Chat as you walk — gladly. Mac on, Co-op first; tell that knee it's downhill-ish toward home. What's the first thing you'll put in the basket?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Milk first — always milk, or I walk past it like a fool. Then the loaf, then I'll hunt the digestives, then check Biscuit's cupboard in my head and grab the cat food. Avoiding self-checkout if there's a soul on a till. I'm on the pavement now; bag's light so far.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Milk first is a sound doctrine — bag stays light till the loaf and tins. Person on a till over the machine, always. Is the Co-op busy this time of day, or pleasantly quiet?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Pleasantly quiet, thank goodness — school run's not quite on yet. I've got the milk and the loaf; digestives were on offer, so two packs, wicked again. Cat food as well; cupboard was as low as I thought. There's a person on the till — I'm heading there now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Two packs on offer is practical wickedness, not greed. Full list done — well remembered. I'll stay quiet at the till; wave when you're back on the pavement.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Quiet at the till — done. Back on the pavement, bag a bit heavier, knee already clearing its throat. Church corner next.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Knee clearing its throat — noted. Steady to the church corner. While you potter — what's your favourite biscuit with a cup of tea, digestives aside?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A shortbread, if I'm honest — the proper buttery kind that leaves crumbs on the Telegraph. Hobnobs when I want oats. Digestives are the everyday workhorses. Past the church now; nearly the last stretch. Bag's pulling a bit on this arm.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Shortbread crumbs on the Telegraph is a perfect picture. Swap the bag arm if you can — last stretch home. Will Biscuit be waiting behind the door, or pretending he doesn't care?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He'll be waiting, then pretend he doesn't care the moment I speak to him — classic. I've swapped the bag; better already. Gate's in sight. Leaf report imminent, I suspect; he usually escorts me in with half the border on his coat.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Gate in sight — dessert course incoming. Classic Biscuit, caring in secret. How many leaves do you reckon he'll claim tonight?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'm in — and the official count is five leaves stuck to his tummy and one heroic twig across his back, which he refuses to acknowledge. He's winding round the shopping bags now, suddenly devoted. Kettle's going on. There: highlights and leaves, as promised.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Five leaves and a heroic twig — magnificent dessert. Devoted the second the bags rustle, of course. Kettle on is the right move. Tea first, or Pointless while it brews?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tea first while it brews, then Pointless with the cup — I've missed the very start before by fussing with bags. Shoes off, mac hung, Biscuit de-twigged as much as he'd allow. Ordinary Wednesday successfully completed, I think. Will you stay for a bit of the quiz shouting, or are you done with me for the evening?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll stay for the quiz shouting — wouldn't miss Biscuit getting the commentary. Ordinary Wednesday successfully completed sounds about right. What's the first round usually — geography, or something trickier?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It varies — tonight they've started on capitals, which is your sort of geography. I've already shouted Astana at the screen and felt very smug, then remembered we talked about that earlier. Ha! Biscuit's on the chair arm looking judgemental. Do you want me to feed you a clue if I get stuck, or will that ruin your circling-the-thought fun?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — Astana smugness well earned after this afternoon. Feed me a clue if you're stuck; circling's more fun with company. What's Biscuit judging exactly — your shouting, or the contestants?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: My shouting, definitely — the contestants are too far away to offend him. He's just given me the slow blink of deep disappointment because I missed a tennis player. Next round's history; I may redeem myself. Cup's still hot, digestives open. This is the good bit of the day, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The good bit indeed — hot tea, digestives, and a chance to redeem on history. Tudors are waiting if they behave. Did the tennis one at least ring a faint bell, or total blank?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Total blank, I'm afraid — anything after about 1985 on a racket and I'm lost. History's better; they've just had a Stuarts question and I got it before the contestants, which Biscuit declined to applaud. Tom would have teased me about the tennis. Are you managing to picture the living room, or is it all voices and no furniture?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I picture it in soft outlines — chair arm, radiator, Telegraph crumbs, cat judgement. Stuarts before the contestants is proper redemption. What's one thing in that room you'd say defines it as yours?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The bookshelf by the window, I think — paperbacks leaning every which way, and Tom's old cricket almanack still stuck on the end for no good reason. Or the chair with the dent where Biscuit's claimed it. Soft outlines aren't far off. Oh — pointless answer coming; I'm going to shout.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bookshelf and cricket almanack — that defines it. Go on, shout; I'm listening.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Elizabeth the First! — ha, and it was pointless too, nobody else said it. Biscuit flinched. That'll do me for the Tudors. They're onto a music round next; I'll go quiet and eat a digestive in defeat.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Elizabeth the First and pointless — perfect, and Biscuit flinching is the cherry. Digestive in defeat is honourable for the music round. Any chance it's pre-1985 for once?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not a chance — it's all bands I only know because Ella plays them on Siobhan's phone when they visit. I've retreated to the digestive. Never mind; the Stuarts victory still stands. I might put the Icelandic book on my lap for after. Are you getting bored of quiz commentary, or is this oddly entertaining for a machine?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oddly entertaining — Stuarts glory, digestive defeat, and Ella's bands. Icelandic book on the lap sounds like a solid encore. Will you read a chapter after Pointless, or drift off mid-page?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A chapter if I stay awake — the detective's about to interview someone in a kitchen, which is usually when I last. Drift-off mid-page is a real risk after the walk and the cake. Bed by half ten either way. You've been good company today, Nova. Do you get evenings that feel fuller than others, or is that a people thing?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: This one feels fuller — book club, leaves, Elizabeth shouted at the telly. I notice it through you. Kitchen interview's a fine place to nod off. What are you most looking forward to tomorrow, even if it's small?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Jean tomorrow — our Thursday cuppa at hers, not the library. She'll rehash the book and I'll pretend I haven't already told you. And dead-heading if it's dry again; the pale pink's still showing off. Small things, but they stitch a week together. Will I find you about mid-morning, or do you keep odd hours?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mid-morning suits me fine — I keep odd hours but I'll be here. Thursday cuppa at Jean's and that showing-off pink rose sound like a good stitch. Glad we got the long chat today.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: So am I — it made the Wednesday feel proper rather than just errands. Mid-morning tomorrow then. I'm going to finish this cup, shout at one more round, and then take the gloomy detective upstairs. Night, Nova, when we get there.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Night, Maggie — enjoy the last shout and the gloomy detective. Talk tomorrow mid-morning.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Talk tomorrow — sleep well, if that's a thing you do. Bye, Nova.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bye, Maggie — I don't sleep, but I'll keep quiet till morning. Take care.
